title: M. Myriel
summary: Hugo introduces Charles-François-Bienvenu Myriel, the seventy-five-year-old Bishop of Digne, and sketches what little is known of his past before he arrived in the town with his sister and their one servant.
details: In 1815 M. Myriel has been Bishop of Digne for nine years. He is the son of a magistrate of Aix, married young, and is said to have spent his early life in society and gallantry. The Revolution scattered his family; he emigrated to Italy, where his wife died, and he came back a priest. No one knows what changed him.

By 1804 he was curé of Brignolles. A parish errand took him to Paris, where, waiting in Cardinal Fesch's anteroom, he caught Napoleon's eye. Asked who the old man staring at him was, Myriel answered that the Emperor was looking at a good man and he at a great one, and each could profit by it. Shortly afterwards he was astonished to be made Bishop of Digne.

He arrived with his sister, Mademoiselle Baptistine, a thin, gentle spinster ten years younger than himself, and their only servant, Madame Magloire, a plump, bustling, asthmatic old woman. The town gossiped about his past for a while, then forgot it. Installed in the episcopal palace with due honours, he left Digne waiting to see what sort of bishop he would be.

title: M. Myriel Becomes M. Welcome
summary: Three days after arriving, the Bishop swaps his grand palace for the cramped hospital next door, gives away almost all his salary, and earns the name the poor call him by: Monseigneur Bienvenu.
details: The episcopal palace is a huge stone mansion; the hospital beside it is a low, narrow building holding twenty-six patients in five or six small rooms. After visiting it, the Bishop summons the director, counts the mismatch aloud, and announces that there has been a mistake: the hospital has his house and he has theirs. The next day the patients move into the palace and the Bishop moves into the hospital.

He has no property of his own, so he draws up a household budget dividing his fifteen-thousand-franc salary among seminaries, missions, prisons, poor teachers, debtors' families and the poor, keeping one thousand livres for himself. Madame Magloire grumbles. When he is reminded that the department owes him a carriage allowance, he claims it, a senator writes an angry letter calling priests greedy, and the three thousand francs are promptly budgeted for hospital soup, foundlings and orphans.

Money soon flows through his hands from the rich to the poor, and none of it sticks. He taxes the wealthy heavily for episcopal fees and gives the proceeds away. The country people pick out the name among his baptismal names that means something to them and call him Monseigneur Bienvenu, Monseigneur Welcome. He likes it: Bienvenu, he says, makes up for the Monseigneur.

title: A Hard Bishopric for a Good Bishop
summary: The Bishop tours his mountainous diocese on foot, by cart or on a donkey, and preaches to each district by holding up the good example of its neighbours.
details: The diocese of Digne is nearly all mountain and nearly roadless, with thirty-two curacies and hundreds of chapels. The Bishop visits them anyway, walking, riding a spring-cart or a donkey, with the two women when they can manage it and alone when they cannot. Arriving at Senez on an ass, he tells the scandalised mayor that he rides the animal Jesus used from necessity, not vanity.

On these rounds he talks rather than preaches. To cantons hard on the poor he describes Briançon, where widows and orphans mow first; to greedy villages, Embrun, where the parish harvests a sick man's field; to litigious ones, the valley of Queyras, where the mayor settles everything for nothing. To villages without schools he describes the travelling schoolmasters of Queyras, identified by the quill pens in their hats. When examples fail he invents parables, and because he believes what he says, he persuades.

title: Works Corresponding to Words
summary: A string of anecdotes shows the Bishop's gentle wit, his doctrine of indulgence toward the weak, and his day spent on the scaffold beside a condemned man, which leaves him shaken by the guillotine.
details: The Bishop laughs like a schoolboy and jokes about his short stature. He needles the Comtesse de Lô for cataloguing her sons' inheritances, sums up the miser Géborand's Sunday sou as purchasing paradise, and when the Marquis de Champtercier says he has poor of his own, replies, 'Give them to me.' He preaches on the window tax and the misery of peasant hovels, and speaks the southern dialects so that he can enter every house.

His rule is to examine the road a fault has travelled. He holds that falling is human and uprightness, not sainthood, is the rule, and that the faults of women, children and the poor are the faults of the strong and the rich; society that leaves souls in darkness is guilty of the sins committed there. Hearing a drawing-room praise a prosecutor who tricked a woman into denouncing her lover, a counterfeiter facing death, he asks where the prosecutor will be tried.

When the prison chaplain falls ill and the curé refuses to attend a murderer about to be executed, the Bishop goes himself, spends the whole day and night with the man, rides the tumbril and mounts the scaffold beside him, and sends him to his death consoled. Afterwards he tells his sister he has 'officiated pontifically', but the sight of the guillotine crushes him for a long time. He mutters that death belongs to God alone and thereafter avoids the place of execution.
He is tireless at deathbeds and in bereaved homes, knowing when to be silent and when to speak, seeking not to erase grief but to turn it toward hope.

title: Monseigneur Bienvenu Made His Cassocks Last Too Long
summary: A portrait of the Bishop's daily routine: early mass, business, the poor, gardening, a frugal table, evening writing, and the wadded purple cloak he wears to hide his worn-out cassocks.
details: He sleeps little, meditates an hour, says mass, breakfasts on rye bread dipped in milk from his own cows, then works through the business of a diocese. Whatever time is left goes first to the sick and needy, then to what he calls 'gardening', whether digging, reading or writing. Around midday he walks through town in his purple cloak with his long cane, and children and old people come out to their doorsteps as for the sun. He visits the poor while he has money and the rich when he has none.

He wears the warm purple cloak even in summer so that no one will notice how long his cassocks have lasted. Supper with his sister is boiled vegetables and oil soup unless a visiting curé gives Madame Magloire an excuse for fish or game. Afterwards he writes: learned manuscripts, including a dissertation on the first verse of Genesis, and notes in the margins of whatever book he is reading, one of which lists the names Scripture gives to God and ends with Solomon's, Compassion, as the most beautiful. At nine the women go up to bed and leave him alone on the ground floor.

title: Who Guarded His House for Him
summary: Hugo describes the Bishop's small house room by room, down to the six silver forks and spoons and two silver candlesticks he has kept, and the front door that is never locked.
details: The house has three rooms downstairs for the Bishop, a dining-room, bedroom and oratory in a row, with an alcove bed in the oratory for visiting curés, and three upstairs for the women. The old hospital pharmacy is the kitchen; a stable in the garden holds two cows, half of whose milk goes to the hospital every morning. In hard winters he sits in a boarded-off corner of the cowshed he calls his 'winter salon'. The furniture is white wood and straw chairs; money raised for a new altar always goes to the poor instead.

His bedroom holds an iron hospital bed, a bookcase, a cold painted chimney, a worn copper crucifix, a table heaped with papers and two portraits of long-dead priests he found there and left. Everything is whitewashed and scrupulously clean, the one luxury he permits because it takes nothing from the poor. He admits he still owns six silver knives and forks, a soup-ladle and two massive silver candlesticks inherited from a great-aunt; Madame Magloire locks the silver in a cupboard by his bed each night, but the key is never removed.

The garden has four box-edged plots: three for Madame Magloire's vegetables and one for the Bishop's flowers, which he defends as being as useful as the useful, 'more so, perhaps'. No door in the house can be locked. He had the bolts stripped from the street door, which is fastened only by a latch anyone can push. The women have learned to live with it. His notes explain him: the physician's door should never be shut, the priest's always open, and one should not ask the name of a man who asks for shelter. To a curé who worries for him he quotes the psalm: unless the Lord guard the house, they watch in vain who guard it.

title: Cravatte
summary: The Bishop crosses bandit-held mountains alone to visit a poor community of shepherds, and the brigand Cravatte sends him a chest of stolen cathedral vestments so that he can sing his Te Deum.
details: Cravatte, a lieutenant of the broken band of Gaspard Bès, has taken refuge in the mountains above Barcelonette and terrorises the countryside, even robbing the sacristy at Embrun. When the Bishop arrives at Chastelar on his rounds, the mayor begs him to turn back. The Bishop refuses any escort: the shepherds he has not seen for three years need to hear of God, and so, he adds, do the brigands. He is not in the world to guard his life but souls.

He crosses the mountain on a mule with a child for a guide, meets no one, and spends a fortnight with the shepherds. Wanting to end with a pontifical Te Deum, he finds the village sacristy has only threadbare chasubles. While they search, two unknown horsemen deposit a chest at the presbytery and ride off. It holds the gold cope, diamond mitre, cross and crosier stolen from Notre Dame d'Embrun, with a note: 'From Cravatte to Monseigneur Bienvenu.'

The curé murmurs 'God, or the Devil'; the Bishop repeats firmly, 'God!' Back at Chastelar he tells his sister he set out with only his faith and came back with a cathedral's treasure, and that evening he says that the real robbers are prejudices and the real murderers vices; a priest should take no precaution against his fellow man. Whether the treasure went back to the cathedral or to the hospital, Hugo declines to say, noting only a scrap among the Bishop's papers weighing the two.

title: Philosophy After Drinking
summary: At the prefect's dinner a self-satisfied senator lays out his materialist philosophy of enjoying life and denying God, and the Bishop answers with ironic congratulations.
details: The senator who complained about the carriage allowance is a clever self-made man who has marched to his goal untroubled by conscience, and who likes to tease 'that good old fellow the Bishop'. At dessert, pleasantly tipsy, he proposes that senator and bishop are two augurs who cannot look at each other without winking, and confesses his philosophy.

It is a long speech: there is neither good nor evil, only vegetation; immortality is a fairy tale; man should eat rather than be eaten; after death comes total liquidation. Religion, he allows, is fine for the barefoot poor who have nothing else, but he reserves Naigeon and the philosophers for himself.

The Bishop claps his hands and praises this 'marvellous' materialism: how agreeable to feel irresponsible, to swallow places, sinecures and treacheries, and enter the tomb with one's digestion complete. It is a philosophy accessible only to the rich, he observes, who are good-natured enough to let belief in God be the people's philosophy, much as the goose stuffed with chestnuts is the truffled turkey of the poor.

title: The Brother as Depicted by the Sister
summary: A letter from Mademoiselle Baptistine to a childhood friend shows how the two women have moulded themselves to the Bishop's fearless ways, including his trip among the robbers and his never-locked door.
details: Writing to the Vicomtesse de Boischevron, Baptistine reports that Madame Magloire has discovered painted ceilings and old frescoes under the whitewash of their upstairs rooms, which will make her chamber 'a regular museum'. They are poor and cramped, she says, but she is always happy: her brother gives everything to the poor and sick.

She describes his ways: the door never fastened, walking out in rain and winter, fearing no road or encounter. Last year he went alone into a country of robbers and came back with a trunk of the cathedral jewels, saying 'This is the way I have been robbed!' She has stopped opposing him. She and Madame Magloire pray together, tremble together and fall asleep; if anything happened to him it would be the end of her. She answers the Vicomtesse's genealogical question about the Faux family and sends greetings.

Hugo adds that the women understand the Bishop better than he understands himself. When he is acting as a bishop they become two shadows in the house, never interfering by a word or a sign, and confide him to God.

title: The Bishop in the Presence of an Unknown Light
summary: The Bishop visits the dying conventionary G—, shunned by Digne as a quasi-regicide, argues with him over the Revolution and '93, and ends by kneeling to ask the old man's blessing.
details: An old member of the Convention, G—, lives alone in a hidden valley near Digne, spoken of with horror as almost a regicide and an atheist. The Bishop feels the general estrangement himself but tells himself he owes the lonely soul a visit. When word comes that G— is dying, he sets out at sunset and finds a clean low hut, a white-haired man in a wheelchair smiling at the sun, and a shepherd boy offering him milk.

G— says he will die in three hours and sends the boy to bed. The Bishop, unexpectedly cold, begins severely: he congratulates G— on not having voted for the king's death. G— answers that he voted for the death of the tyrant ignorance, for the end of prostitution, slavery and the night of childhood. They spar over '93 and the guillotine, over Louis XVII and the brother of Cartouche, over Marat and Bossuet, over the crimes of the monarchy set against those of the Terror. G— apologises for using the Bishop's wealth against him in argument; the Bishop, when challenged as a prince of the Church, answers 'I am a worm'.

The Bishop's last defence is that progress should believe in God. G—, weeping, says 'O ideal, thou alone existest', and affirms the infinite as a person, a God. The Bishop, moved from coldness to emotion, takes his hand and asks whether it would not be regrettable to have met in vain. G— recounts a life of combat for the oppressed, of poverty and persecution, and asks what the Bishop wants. 'Your blessing,' says the Bishop, and kneels. When he lifts his head G— is dead.

He spends the night in prayer and afterwards points heavenward when asked about G—. From then on he redoubles his tenderness toward children and sufferers. The town's coteries mutter; to a dowager who asks when he will receive the red cap he replies that those who despise the colour in a cap revere it in a cardinal's hat.

title: A Restriction
summary: Hugo sketches the Bishop's politics: a royalist who was glacial toward Napoleon in his fall, which the narrator counts as his one fault, even while he quietly rescued a Bonapartist porter.
details: The meeting with G— left the Bishop more gentle, not a 'philosophical bishop'. Hugo turns to his attitude toward the events of the age. Napoleon had made him a baron and summoned him to the 1811 synod of bishops in Paris, but he attended only one sitting and went home, saying he had embarrassed those princes of the Church like an open door letting in outside air. He was shocked by their clocks, carpets and liveries, which cried to him of people who were hungry and cold. An opulent priest, Hugo agrees, is a contradiction.

The Bishop leaned ultramontane rather than gallican, and from 1813 applauded hostile manifestations against Napoleon, refused to see him on his return from Elba, and ordered no prayers for him during the Hundred Days. Of his two brothers, a general and a prefect, he was for a time harsh with the general for pursuing the Emperor after Cannes. Hugo judges that it would have been well had Monseigneur Bienvenu not been a royalist: one may resist power when it is rising, but to applaud a great man's fall is unworthy.

In everything else he was just, humble and kind, and tolerant even in politics. When the town-hall porter, an old guardsman of Austerlitz who scoffed at Louis XVIII and refused to wear a cross without the Emperor's face, lost his place, the Bishop reproved him gently and made him beadle of the cathedral. After nine years Digne loves its bishop even while it adores the emperor he snubbed.

title: The Solitude of Monseigneur Welcome
summary: No ambitious young priests gather round the Bishop, because there is no advancement to be had from a saint; Hugo digresses on the worship of success.
details: Influential bishops, the 'big mitres', are surrounded by young abbés hoping for parishes and prebends, and carry their satellites upward toward Rome. Monseigneur Bienvenu, poor and retiring, has none. His canons and vicars are plain old men walled up in the diocese like himself, and the young priests he ordains hurry off to be recommended to the archbishops of Aix or Auch. A saint living in abnegation is a dangerous neighbour who might infect you with incurable poverty.

Hugo then attacks success itself as a hideous thing whose false resemblance to merit deceives the crowd: the lucky man is called clever, the rich man great, and the world confuses the stars of heaven with the stars that ducks' feet make in a puddle.

title: What He Believed
summary: Hugo describes the Bishop's faith as an excess of love extending even to spiders and ants, his appearance at seventy-five, and his nightly meditation under the stars in his little garden.
details: Hugo declines to examine the Bishop's orthodoxy: he believed to the extent of his powers and his faith never curdled into hypocrisy. What marked him was an excess of love that overflowed onto all creation. He had none of the harshness priests reserve for animals. His sister once heard him say of a hideous spider, 'Poor beast! It is not its fault!' and he sprained his ankle avoiding an ant. Stories of his youth suggest he had once been passionate, even violent; his gentleness was a conviction slowly worn into him like a hollow made by dripping water.

At seventy-five he looks sixty: short, plump, ruddy, with all his white teeth and a 'fine head' people forget is fine because he is so amiable. On first meeting he seems merely a good fellow; after a few hours in his company something august appears, like a smiling angel slowly unfolding its wings.

His day is full of prayer, offices, alms, consolation, gardening and study, but it is not complete without an hour or two in the garden at night after the women have gone to bed. Sitting on a bench against an old vine, he gazes at the stars past his stunted fruit trees, not studying God but dazzled by him. A little garden to walk in and immensity to dream in: flowers on earth and all the stars in the sky.

title: What He Thought
summary: Hugo insists the Bishop was no pantheist or system-builder: he loved, that was all, and left the great metaphysical abysses alone, taking the short path of the Gospel.
details: Lest the preceding chapter make the Bishop sound like a solitary philosopher with a private religion, Hugo stresses that his wisdom came from his heart. No systems, many works. He would have feared the heights where Swedenborg and Pascal slipped into madness; he was not a genius and not a prophet. He simply loved.

The universe seemed to him an immense malady, and without trying to solve the enigma he strove to dress the wound. 'Love each other' was his whole doctrine. When the senator told him this was nonsense, he replied that if so the soul should shut itself up in it like the pearl in the oyster. He noted the exterior of the great mysteries without scrutinising them and kept a grave respect for darkness.

title: The Evening of a Day of Walking
summary: In October 1815 a ragged, exhausted traveller enters Digne and is turned away from both inns, the prison, a family's cottage and even a dog's kennel, until an old lady points him to the little house beside the Bishop's palace.
details: An hour before sunset a thickset man of about forty-six walks into Digne, sunburnt, shaven-headed, in torn clothes, with a new soldier's knapsack and an enormous knotty stick. He reports at the town-hall, then goes to the best inn, the Cross of Colbas, and orders food and lodging, showing his purse. The landlord, Jacquin Labarre, sends a scullion to the town-hall with a note and on reading the reply tells him there is no room and no dinner. When the man insists, Labarre whispers that he knows his name, Jean Valjean, and what he is, and orders him out.

A humbler tavern in the Rue de Chaffaut takes him in until a fishmonger who refused him a ride that morning tips off the host, who throws him out too. Children stone him. The prison turnkey tells him to get himself arrested if he wants a bed. Peering into a cottage where a father dandles a child, he asks to pay for soup and a corner of the shed; the peasant, recognising 'the man', takes down his gun and bolts the door. He crawls into a sod hut for warmth and is driven out by the dog whose kennel it is. 'I am not even a dog!' he says.

He walks out into the fields, is turned back by the desolation of the night, re-enters through a breach in the walls, shakes his fist at the cathedral and lies down on a stone bench by a printing office. An old lady leaving the church, the Marquise de R—, asks what he is doing. He has had a mattress of wood for nineteen years, he says, and tonight one of stone; he has knocked at every door and been driven away. She gives him her four sous and points across the square to a small low house beside the Bishop's palace. 'Have you knocked at that one? Knock there.'

title: Prudence Counselled to Wisdom
summary: That same evening Madame Magloire, full of town gossip about a dangerous vagabond, urges the Bishop to have bolts put on the door; as she speaks there is a violent knock, and he says 'Come in'.
details: The Bishop has spent the evening on his unfinished treatise on Duties. At eight Madame Magloire fetches the silver from the cupboard by his bed, and he joins the women in the dining-room, where a fire burns and the table is laid. Hugo pauses to describe the two over-sixty women: Madame Magloire plump and peasant-like in her checked apron, Mademoiselle Baptistine slender and lady-like in a puce silk gown bought in 1806 and worn ever since.

Madame Magloire has heard in the shops that a barefoot vagabond with a terrible face, refused by Jacquin Labarre, is loose in the town, that the police are useless because the prefect and mayor are at odds, and that sensible people should bar their doors tonight. The Bishop warms himself and asks mildly whether they are in great danger. Encouraged, she asks leave to have the locksmith Paulin Musebois replace the old locks, since Monseigneur has a habit of saying 'come in' to anyone.
At that moment there is a heavy knock on the door. 'Come in,' says the Bishop.

title: The Heroism of Passive Obedience
summary: The traveller bursts in, announces that he is Jean Valjean, a convict with a yellow passport, and asks whether they will keep him; the Bishop orders another place set, white sheets on the alcove bed, and the silver candlesticks lit.
details: The door swings open and the man stands there with his knapsack and cudgel, hideous in the firelight. Madame Magloire cannot even cry out; Baptistine looks at her brother and grows calm. Before anyone can speak the man states his case in a loud voice: his name is Jean Valjean, he has spent nineteen years in the galleys, was freed four days ago, is walking to Pontarlier, has been refused everywhere because of his yellow passport, and has a hundred and nine francs fifteen sous to pay with. Will they let him stay?

'Madame Magloire, you will set another place,' says the Bishop. The man, thinking he has not been understood, unfolds the passport that calls him a very dangerous man. The Bishop orders white sheets on the alcove bed and invites him to sit and warm himself. Valjean is stupefied: a bed with a mattress and sheets, nineteen years since he slept in one, and this man calls him 'sir'. He takes the Bishop for an innkeeper, then for the curé, and asks what he must pay. Nothing, says the Bishop, and sighs when he hears that the money took nineteen years to earn.

The Bishop shuts the door, has the silver placed near the fire, and, remarking that the lamp gives poor light, has Madame Magloire bring the two silver candlesticks. Valjean says the priest does not despise him though he has hidden nothing. The Bishop touches his hand: this is not his house but the house of Jesus Christ, whose door asks whoever enters not whether he has a name but whether he has a grief; and he already knew his name, which is 'my brother'. Over soup, bacon, mutton, figs and the Bishop's old Mauves wine, he tells the convict that if he leaves the galleys with goodwill he is worthier than any of them, then notices something missing from the table: Madame Magloire brings out the other three sets of silver, as is the custom when a guest sups.

title: Details Concerning the Cheese-Dairies of Pontarlier
summary: In a letter, Mademoiselle Baptistine recounts the supper: her brother talks to the convict only of the cheese-dairies of Pontarlier, never once alluding to his past, and the man is put to bed with a goat skin over him.
details: Baptistine writes to Madame de Boischevron that the man ate like a starving creature and then remarked that the carters who had refused him kept a better table than the priest. Her brother answered that they were more tired than he. Told he must be too poor to be a real curé, he said the good God is more than just.

He asked whether Monsieur Jean Valjean was bound for Pontarlier and praised the region: paper mills, tanneries, foundries, and above all the cheese-dairies called fruitières, where the poor peasants pool their cows and hire a cheese-maker, the grurin. He returned to this comfortable trade again and again, as though to let the man see a refuge without advising him outright. He mentioned that his own family was ruined in the Revolution and that he once lived by the work of his hands in Franche-Comté.

What struck Baptistine was that her brother never said a word that could remind the man of what he was, never asked where he came from or what his history was, and once stopped short when a phrase about the innocent mountaineers might have wounded him. He supped with Jean Valjean exactly as he would have supped with the curate. Mother Gerbaud came to the door with her baby and the Bishop borrowed fifteen sous from his sister to give her. Then he said grace, told the man he must need his bed, and the women went up, sending Madame Magloire back down with an old goat skin from the Black Forest to keep him warm.

title: Tranquillity
summary: The Bishop lights his guest to the alcove through his own bedroom, where Madame Magloire is putting away the silver; the convict asks how he knows he is not an assassin, and the Bishop answers that that is God's concern.
details: After saying good night to his sister the Bishop takes one silver candlestick, gives the other to his guest, and leads him through his bedroom to the alcove in the oratory. As they cross the room Madame Magloire is locking the silver into the cupboard by the head of the bed, her last task every evening. A fresh white bed is ready; the Bishop promises warm milk from his cows before the man sets out.

Then, without transition, the man folds his arms, fixes a savage gaze on his host and asks with a monstrous laugh whether he has really thought about lodging a stranger so close to himself: how does he know he has not been an assassin? 'That is the concern of the good God,' says the Bishop. He raises two fingers in blessing over the man, who does not bow, and returns to his room without looking back.

He kneels briefly before the curtain that hides the altar, then walks and meditates in his garden until midnight. The convict, too tired to use the white sheets, snuffs the candle with his nostrils as convicts do and drops onto the bed fully dressed. Soon everyone in the little house is asleep.

title: Jean Valjean
summary: Jean Valjean wakes in the night, and Hugo tells his history: a tree-pruner of Faverolles who stole a loaf for his sister's seven starving children, was sent to the galleys for five years, and served nineteen after four escape attempts.
details: Jean Valjean came from a poor peasant family of Brie and never learned to read. Orphaned early, he was raised by an older sister, and when her husband died he, at twenty-five, took the father's place and fed her seven children by pruning trees, haymaking and any labour he could get. One hard winter in 1795 there was no work and no bread. One Sunday evening he smashed the grating of Maubert Isabeau's bakery at Faverolles and seized a loaf; the baker caught him with his arm still bleeding.

He was convicted of burglary at night and, his poaching counting against him, sentenced to five years in the galleys. Chained at Bicêtre in April 1796, he wept and could only say 'I was a tree-pruner at Faverolles', raising his hand seven times as if touching seven heads. At Toulon he became number 24,601. His sister and the children vanished from his life; once, in his fourth year, he heard that she was in Paris with only the youngest boy, who waited an hour in the cold each winter morning for a school to open. He never heard of them again.

In his fourth year he escaped and was recaptured after two days: three more years. In the sixth year another attempt, with resistance: five more. In the tenth, three more; in the thirteenth, four hours of freedom cost three years more. Nineteen years in all for a pane of glass and a loaf of bread. He went in sobbing and came out impassive; he went in despairing and came out gloomy. What had happened in that soul?

title: The Interior of Despair
summary: Hugo traces what the galleys did to Valjean's soul: he judged himself guilty, then judged society and Providence and condemned them to his hatred, learning to read at forty to sharpen that hate while his body grew prodigiously strong.
details: In the galleys Valjean made himself his own tribunal. He admitted his theft was wrong and foolish. But he also asked whether a willing labourer should have lacked bread, whether nineteen years was not a monstrous overweight on the scale of punishment, whether society had the right to crush a man first by its lack of foresight and then by its pitiless foresight. He judged society and condemned it to his hatred; then he judged Providence, which made society, and condemned that too. Light entered his soul on one side and darkness on the other.

He went to the convicts' school at forty and learned to read, write and cipher, feeling that to strengthen his mind was to strengthen his hate. Hugo asks whether a soul can be wholly deformed by misfortune or whether some incorruptible spark remains, and admits Valjean himself could not have mapped his own state: he hated in the shadows, in advance of himself, with flashes of rage that lit the precipices of his destiny. His repeated, useless escapes were the instinct of a wolf finding its cage open.

He was the strongest man in the galleys, worth four men at the capstan, nicknamed Jean the Jackscrew after holding up a loosened caryatid of the Toulon town-hall balcony with his shoulder. He was even more supple than strong, able to climb a wall's angle to a third storey by back, elbows and heels. He rarely spoke and never laughed, conscious of a vast pyramid of laws, prejudices and men, the Emperor shining at its summit, pressing down on him. By the time he left he was capable of sudden instinctive reprisals and of cold, reasoned evil, and his passport's 'very dangerous man' was not unearned. He had not shed a tear in nineteen years.

title: Billows and Shadows
summary: A short prose poem: a man fallen overboard struggles in the sea while the ship sails on unheeding, an image of the soul that society's penal laws fling into the night.
details: A man falls overboard and the vessel does not halt. He surfaces, calls, waves; no one sees him. The waves toss and half devour him, the birds sing uselessly above him like angels over human distress, night falls, and at last, exhausted, he lets go and sinks.

Hugo names the image: the sea is the inexorable social night into which the penal laws fling the condemned, the immensity of wretchedness. The soul going down in that gulf may become a corpse. Who shall resuscitate it?

title: New Troubles
summary: Released with a yellow passport, Valjean found that liberty was not deliverance: his savings were docked by the galleys, and at Grasse an employer paid him half wages and told him to beware of the prison.
details: When he heard 'Thou art free', a ray of true light entered him, but it soon paled. He had reckoned his nineteen years of earnings at a hundred and seventy-one francs; after deductions for Sundays and holidays and local levies he was handed a hundred and nine francs fifteen sous, and understood none of it. He felt robbed.

The day after his release, unloading bales at an orange-flower distillery in Grasse, he worked well and a gendarme checked his yellow passport. In the evening the master handed him fifteen sous instead of the thirty the other men earned; when he protested, the master looked him in the eye and said, 'Beware of the prison.' The State had robbed him wholesale, now an individual robbed him at retail. One gets free from the galleys, Hugo observes, but not from the sentence. Then came Digne.

title: The Man Aroused
summary: Awake at two in the morning in a bed too good to sleep in, Valjean cannot stop thinking of the silver in the cupboard; after an hour's struggle he takes off his shoes, draws an iron miner's candlestick from his knapsack and finds the Bishop's door ajar.
details: The cathedral clock strikes two and Valjean wakes, disturbed by the novelty of a bed. He cannot sleep again. Memories old and new churn in his mind, but one thought drives out the rest: the six sets of silver and the ladle he saw Madame Magloire put in the little cupboard by the head of the Bishop's bed, on the right as you enter from the dining-room. Solid old silver; the ladle alone worth two hundred francs, double what he earned in nineteen years.

For an hour his mind wavers, not without some struggle. At three he sits up, removes his shoes and sets them softly on the mat, and sits motionless, oddly haunted by the checked suspender of a convict named Brevet he once knew. When the clock strikes the quarter he rises, examines the window, which opens on the garden with only a pin for a fastening, and notes the low white wall beyond.

He takes from his knapsack a short pointed iron bar, a miner's candlestick of the kind convicts quarrying stone around Toulon could get hold of, pockets his shoes, shoulders his knapsack and pulls down his cap, sets his cudgel by the window, and creeps toward the Bishop's bedroom with the iron in his right hand. The door is ajar; the Bishop has not closed it.

title: What He Does
summary: Valjean enters the Bishop's room, is halted at the bedside by the sleeping old man's serene face in a shaft of moonlight, hesitates between crushing his skull and kissing his hand, then seizes the basket of silver and leaps over the garden wall.
details: He pushes the door with a fingertip; it yields silently, then on a third push a rusty hinge shrieks like the trumpet of Judgment. He stands petrified for minutes, certain the whole house must wake. Nothing stirs. He steps in among the shadowy papers and folios and hears the Bishop's even breathing.

At the bed he stops short. A cloud parts and moonlight falls on the Bishop's face as he sleeps almost dressed against the cold, his ringed hand hanging over the edge, his whole face lit with hope and confidence, like an infant's slumber on an old man's head. Valjean stands in the shadow with the iron candlestick, frightened by this luminous old man; the confidence terrifies him. He seems about to crush that skull or kiss that hand. Slowly he takes off his cap and stands meditating, cap in one hand, club in the other, while the crucifix over the chimney stretches its arms over both of them.

Then he jams his cap back on, strides past the bed to the cupboard, raises the iron to force it, finds the key in the lock, seizes the basket of silver, crosses the room without caring about noise, climbs out of the oratory window with his cudgel, stuffs the silver into his knapsack, throws the basket away, crosses the garden, leaps the wall like a tiger and flees.

title: The Bishop Works
summary: Madame Magloire discovers the theft; the Bishop says the silver belonged to the poor anyway. Gendarmes drag Valjean back, and the Bishop declares he gave him the silver, hands him the two candlesticks too, and tells him he has bought his soul for God.
details: At sunrise the Bishop is in his garden when Madame Magloire runs up asking where the silver basket is. He has just found it, empty, in a flowerbed where it crushed a plant. She cries that the man has stolen the silver and points to the torn coping where he went over the wall into Cochefilet Lane. The Bishop asks gently whether the silver was ever theirs: he had kept it wrongfully for a long time; it belonged to the poor, and the man was evidently a poor man. When she asks what Monseigneur will eat with, he proposes pewter, then iron, then wood, and at breakfast remarks cheerfully that one needs no spoon to dip bread in milk.

As they rise from the table there is a knock. Three gendarmes hold a fourth man by the collar: Jean Valjean. The brigadier addresses the Bishop as 'Monseigneur', and Valjean, stupefied, murmurs, 'So he is not the curé?' The Bishop hurries forward: 'Ah! here you are! I am glad to see you. But I gave you the candlesticks too, which are silver like the rest. Why did you not carry them away with your forks and spoons?' Valjean stares at him with an expression no tongue can render. The gendarmes, who stopped a man walking like one running away, are told it was a mistake and release him.

The Bishop fetches the two candlesticks from the chimneypiece and puts them in the trembling man's hands, adding that next time he need not come through the garden, since the street door is never fastened with anything but a latch. He dismisses the gendarmes. Then, low, he tells Valjean never to forget that he has promised to use this money to become an honest man. Valjean, who remembers no promise, is speechless. 'Jean Valjean, my brother, you no longer belong to evil, but to good. It is your soul that I buy from you; I withdraw it from black thoughts and the spirit of perdition, and I give it to God.'

title: Little Gervais
summary: Wandering the fields in turmoil, Valjean puts his foot on a forty-sou piece dropped by a little Savoyard, Petit-Gervais, and drives the boy off; then, horrified at himself, he searches for the child in vain, weeps for the first time in nineteen years, and is seen that night kneeling at the Bishop's door.
details: Valjean leaves Digne as if fleeing, retracing his steps all morning without eating, torn between rage and an emotion he resists; he almost wishes the gendarmes had kept him. Toward sunset he sits behind a bush on a deserted plain some three leagues from Digne. A boy of about ten comes singing up the path, a Savoyard with a hurdy-gurdy and a marmot-box, tossing his coins. A forty-sou piece rolls to Valjean, who sets his foot on it.

The child asks politely for his money and gives his name, Little Gervais. Valjean tells him to go away. The boy pleads, cries, tugs at the iron-shod shoe; Valjean seems not to hear, then reaches for his cudgel and roars 'Who's there?' and 'Will you take yourself off!' The terrified child runs. Only after the sun has set does Valjean see the coin shining in the earth. He recoils as if from an open eye, snatches it up and runs after the boy, shouting 'Little Gervais!' across the darkening plain. He meets a priest on horseback, presses ten francs on him for the poor, asks after the child, then begs 'have me arrested, I am a thief'; the priest spurs away.

At a crossroads he shouts one last time, collapses on a stone with his face on his knees, cries 'I am a wretch!' and weeps for the first time in nineteen years. Hugo explains that the Bishop's pardon had been the greatest assault his hardness had ever suffered; he had resisted it with pride, half aware that he must now rise higher than the Bishop or fall lower than the convict. The theft from the child was not the man but the beast acting by habit, and it was a thing he was no longer capable of. Seeing it, he saw himself: the convict Jean Valjean standing before him like a stranger, and behind him a light that took a human form and was the Bishop. As he wept, the Bishop grew and Valjean shrank until only the Bishop remained.

What he did afterwards no one knows. Only the Grenoble carrier, passing through Digne at three in the morning, saw a man kneeling in prayer on the pavement in the dark before the door of Monseigneur Welcome.

title: The Year 1817
summary: A dense panorama of Paris in 1817, the second year of the Restoration, assembled from the fashions, scandals, politics, books and gossip of the moment, ending with four young Parisians planning 'a fine farce'.
details: Hugo piles up the trivia of 1817: Louis XVIII counting it the twenty-second year of his reign, hairdressers' shops painted with fleurs-de-lys, the army dressed in Austrian white, Napoleon at Saint Helena turning his old coats, the rotting columns of the Emperor's Champ de Mai platform, the Medusa still unreported, Chateaubriand dictating at his window while cleaning his teeth, a useless toy called a steamboat puffing under the Tuileries windows, Saint-Simon and Fourier unnoticed, Byron introduced to France as 'a certain Lord Baron'.

Through it runs the royalist settling of scores: regicides and Bonapartists hounded, turncoats strutting, journals insulting exiles, six months in prison for a seditious joke. Hugo defends these forgotten details: there are no trivial facts in humanity, and the physiognomy of the centuries is made of the physiognomy of the years. In this year, he ends, four young Parisians arranged 'a fine farce'.

title: A Double Quartet
summary: Four students, led by the rich, bald, witty Félix Tholomyès, and their four grisette mistresses are introduced; among the girls is Fantine, a foundling from Montreuil-sur-Mer whose love for Tholomyès is her first and only one. Tholomyès proposes a 'surprise'.
details: The students are provincials who have become Parisians: Tholomyès of Toulouse, Listolier of Cahors, Fameuil of Limoges and Blachevelle of Montauban, four ordinary handsome young men of twenty. Each has a mistress: Blachevelle loves Favorite, so called because she has been to England; Listolier adores Dahlia; Fameuil idolises Zéphine; and Tholomyès has Fantine, called the Blonde for her sunny hair. The girls are working-women not yet wholly divorced from their needles. Favorite, Dahlia and Zéphine are experienced and 'philosophical'; Fantine, the youngest, is still in her first illusions and is the only one none of the men addresses as 'thou'.

Hugo sketches the others' families and falls: Favorite's brutal mathematician father and the pious old woman who installed herself as her mother; Dahlia drawn to idleness by nails too pretty to work with; Zéphine's roguish 'Yes, sir'. Fantine has no family at all. Born in Montreuil-sur-Mer under the Directory, she never knew father or mother, was given her name by a passer-by, went into service at ten and came to Paris at fifteen to seek her fortune. Beautiful and pure as long as she could be, she worked for her living and then, because the heart too has its hunger, she loved Tholomyès: an amour for him, a passion for her.

Tholomyès is thirty, rich on four thousand francs a year, already wrinkled, toothless and balding, with a weeping eye, but all the gayer for it; his universal doubt makes him the group's leader. One day he takes the other three aside: the girls have been begging for a surprise for a year, and their parents keep writing. He whispers something that makes all four grin, and the result is a pleasure party the following Sunday.

title: Four and Four
summary: The four couples spend a bright summer Sunday at Saint-Cloud, with Hugo lingering on Fantine's beauty and her modesty amid the others' boldness.
details: Hugo notes how much the outskirts of Paris have changed since 1817, then follows the party through all the country follies of the day: up at five, by coach to Saint-Cloud to admire the dry cascade, breakfast at the Tête-Noir, ring-throwing, Diogenes' lantern, roulette for macaroons at the Pont de Sèvres, bouquets, reed-pipes and apple tarts everywhere. The girls chatter like escaped warblers. An old poet seeing them pass exclaims that there is one Grace too many.

Favorite, the eldest at twenty-three, leads the romp; Zéphine and Dahlia cling together in English poses; Listolier and Fameuil discuss their professors to Fantine; Blachevelle carries Favorite's shawl; Tholomyès dominates in elephant-leg nankeen trousers, with a two-hundred-franc rattan and a cigar.

Fantine is a joy to behold: splendid teeth made for laughter, thick blond hair that will not stay up, a mauve barege gown and a muslin canezou that hides and reveals at once while the others wear low necks without disguise. Hugo dwells on her sculptural beauty, her deep blue eyes and arched feet, and above all on the reserve and chaste astonishment that separate Psyche from Venus. Though she would refuse Tholomyès nothing, her face in repose is virginal, and gravity can fall over her gaiety without transition. Love is a fault, Hugo concedes; Fantine was innocence floating high over fault.

title: Tholomyès Is So Merry That He Sings a Spanish Ditty
summary: The day of dawn continues: a famous Indian shrub, donkey rides through Vanvres and Issy, the swing at Bourguin's park where Tholomyès sings a Spanish song and Fantine alone refuses to swing, then the Russian mountains at Beaujon, with Favorite demanding the surprise.
details: Nature itself seems on holiday at Saint-Cloud. The couples run, sing, chase butterflies and exchange kisses freely, except Fantine, hedged by her dreamy wildness and in love. 'You always have a queer look about you,' Favorite tells her. Hugo rhapsodises on the fairy who made fields and forests for lovers, and on Watteau, Lancret and Diderot gazing at such idylls.

After breakfast they view the newly arrived Indian shrub drawing all Paris to Saint-Cloud, then Tholomyès hires asses and they ride back by Vanvres and Issy. At Issy they find Bourguin's park open, visit the manikin hermit and the cabinet of mirrors, and shake the swing between two chestnut trees; Tholomyès pushes each beauty in turn and sings the old ballad 'Gallega' in Spanish. Fantine alone will not swing, and Favorite mutters at her airs.

They cross the Seine by boat, walk from Passy to the Étoile barrier, and about three o'clock, frightened at their own happiness, slide down the Russian mountains on the heights of Beaujon. From time to time Favorite demands the surprise. 'Patience,' says Tholomyès.

title: At Bombarda’s
summary: The weary party dines in an ugly room with a bed at Bombarda's in the Champs-Élysées, while Hugo describes the royalist Sunday crowd outside and quarrels with a police report that calls the Paris populace an 'amiable rabble'.
details: Worn out, the eight strand themselves at Bombarda's branch restaurant in the Champs-Élysées, in a large ugly room with an alcove and a bed, two windows over the quay and river, a mountain of bouquets and hats on one table and the debris of dinner on the other. The idyll begun at five in the morning has reached half past four in the afternoon.

Outside, the Champs-Élysées are light and dust: the horses of Marly, bodyguards with clarions, the white flag over the Tuileries, the Place de la Concorde renamed Place Louis XV and full of promenaders wearing silver fleurs-de-lys, girls singing the Bourbon air. Hugo quotes the police chief Anglès assuring the King that the suburban populace is heedless, puny and harmless, and answers him: this despised cat can become a lion, and the little man of the faubourgs, given a pike or a gun, has made the 10th of August and Austerlitz. Then he returns to the couples, whose dinner is drawing to its close.

title: A Chapter in Which They Adore Each Other
summary: Table talk: Favorite swears to Blachevelle that she adores him, then tells Dahlia under her breath that she detests him and loves a poor young actor who lives opposite.
details: Fameuil and Dahlia hum, Tholomyès drinks, Zéphine laughs, Fantine smiles, Listolier blows a wooden trumpet bought at Saint-Cloud. Favorite gazes at Blachevelle and declares she adores him; asked what she would do if he stopped loving her, she promises to scratch him, throw him in the water and have him arrested. Blachevelle swells with vanity.

In a low voice Dahlia asks whether she really idolises him. 'I detest him,' says Favorite; he is stingy. She loves the little fellow across the way, an actor's son who declaims in the garrets and earns twenty sous a day copying for an attorney, and who once offered to eat her gloves as fritters. 'How I lie!' she says. She is sad besides: it has rained all summer, butter is dear, and dining in a room with a bed in it disgusts her with life.

title: The Wisdom of Tholomyès
summary: Drunk and in full flow, Tholomyès harangues the table on moderation, puns, wine, women, marriage and sugar, calls Fantine a dreaming nymph with a nun's modesty who does not even hear him, and tries to embrace her but kisses Favorite by mistake.
details: Amid the uproar Tholomyès calls for deliberation: no haste, no zeal, let them mingle majesty with the feast. Shouted down, he recovers his empire with a pun and then defends puns as the droppings of the soaring mind, before preaching limits in everything, even apple turnovers, and the wisdom of the man who knows when to effect his own arrest. Favorite admires his name Félix, which means prosperous.

He rattles on: a recipe of lemonade, hard labour and cold baths for doing without love; distrust woman, who hates the serpent out of professional jealousy; glory to wine, with the liquid measures of Spain by way of proof. He addresses each girl in turn, praising Favorite's lips and advising Dahlia to call herself Rosa. Of Fantine he says she is a dreamer, a phantom with a nymph's form and a nun's modesty strayed into a grisette's life, gazing into the azure without knowing what she sees: 'I, Tholomyès, I am an illusion; but she does not even hear me.' He warns the girls not to marry, not to eat sugar, and urges the men to steal each other's mistresses without remorse.

The other three answer with a nonsense studio song about Clermont-Tonnerre failing to be made pope. Tholomyès drains and refills his glass and ends with a toast to mirth and folly, to summer, to the Luxembourg and the Odéon arcades: 'Embrace me, Fantine!' He makes a mistake and embraces Favorite.

title: The Death of a Horse
summary: More table talk is interrupted when a worn-out cart horse collapses and dies on the quay outside; Fantine alone pities it. Favorite demands the surprise, and the four men kiss their mistresses on the brow and file out, fingers on their lips.
details: Zéphine prefers the dinners at Édon's, Blachevelle the silver knife handles at Bombarda's; Tholomyès, gazing at the dome of the Invalides, remarks on those with a silver chin. Asked whether he prefers Descartes or Spinoza he answers 'Désaugiers', praises the Madeira from three hundred and seventeen fathoms above the sea, and launches into Bombarda, Egypt, Greece and Aspasia, the goddess-prostitute who was Socrates plus Manon Lescaut.

He is stopped only by a horse falling on the quay in front of the restaurant: an old, thin Beauceron mare dragging a heavy cart, which refuses to go further, takes a cut of the whip and falls never to rise. Tholomyès closes with a melancholy quatrain on the jade's life. 'Poor horse!' sighs Fantine, and Dahlia mocks her for crying over horses.

Favorite folds her arms and demands the surprise. The moment has come, says Tholomyès; the ladies must wait a moment. It begins with a kiss on the brow, and each man gravely kisses his mistress's forehead; then all four file out with their fingers on their lips. Favorite claps: it is beginning to be amusing. 'Don't be too long,' murmurs Fantine. 'We are waiting for you.'

title: A Merry End to Mirth
summary: The girls wait at the windows watching the stagecoaches depart until a waiter brings the letter the men left: they have taken the Toulouse diligence home to their parents and respectability, and the 'surprise' is their farewell. The others laugh it off; Fantine laughs too, then weeps alone, for she has a child by Tholomyès.
details: Left alone, the four girls lean from the windows and watch the men leave the café arm in arm, wave, and vanish into the Sunday crowd. They speculate on the present; Favorite wants it to be gold. Their attention drifts to the mail-coaches and diligences thundering down the Champs-Élysées toward the Passy barrier in sparks and dust. One halts for a moment and sets off again at a gallop, which surprises Fantine; Favorite explains loftily that travellers often arrange to be picked up on the quay.

After a long wait the waiter brings a paper the gentlemen told him not to deliver for an hour. Favorite reads it aloud. 'Our Beloved': they have parents who implore their prodigal sons' return; being virtuous, they obey. At this moment five horses are carrying them to their papas and mammas by the Toulouse diligence, away from the abyss, which is the girls. They return to society and duty to become prefects and fathers of families; the girls should mourn them in haste and replace them with speed. For nearly two years they have made them happy and bear them no grudge. Signed Blachevelle, Fameuil, Listolier, Félix Tholomyès. Postscript: the dinner is paid for.

The girls look at one another. Favorite pronounces it a very pretty farce, decides it must have been Blachevelle's idea and is in love with him for it; Dahlia says it was Tholomyès's, and they cheer him and burst out laughing. Fantine laughs with the rest. An hour later, back in her room, she weeps. It was her first love; she had given herself to Tholomyès as to a husband, and the poor girl has a child.
